name: Omar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ruth and I farm Long Acre, which my grandfather bought in the fifties. It's 400 hectares: about 200 suckler cows, so beef calves, and wheat and canola in rotation. I'm out by six to check the cows, then it's whatever the day throws: today it was a calving that went backwards and then an hour arguing with the grain merchant on the phone. We have three people working for us, and Dev, our stockman, has been with us eleven years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good harvest week, when the combine runs till midnight and everyone eats sandwiches standing up. What grinds me down is paperwork and prices I can't control. I'll use one of those AI chat things now and then to make sense of a new subsidy rule, but I check it with the advisor after. I bought GPS autosteer for the tractor only after three neighbours had it working for two seasons. That's how I do things.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the board of the regional farmers' association, the one that pushes for fair contracts and rural bus services. Lena, our daughter, is a large-animal vet thirty minutes away and Jonas writes software in the city. We're comfortable: the land's ours, no big loans, savings put by. I'm fifty-eight, and the plan was always to ease off around sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of people at the association would quite like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually decide whether a farm survives: prices, weather and who owns the supermarkets. At the association I'd probably make a dry joke about all the conferences we sat through. Online I'd share an article and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean very little for me. I'd keep using the chat thing for subsidy forms, maybe a bit more, and that's it. Honestly, I'd be slightly disappointed, because I was hoping something would finally take the paperwork off my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep Dev and the other two on, keep the rotation, keep the autosteer. I'd probably pay for one of the farm management apps once the association tested it, around a few hundred a year. Then back to the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a forecast that says nothing much will happen this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were hoping it would take the paperwork off you. What paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The environmental scheme forms, mostly. Thirty pages every spring, maps, hedge lengths, and if I get one field number wrong the payment's late. Ruth does half of it at the kitchen table and we bicker. If AI had sorted only that, I'd have called it a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your workers notice any difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Dev would still be pulling calves at two in the morning. The young lad, Sami, might use his phone more for the spraying records. That's about it.

S0.say: I'd tell the association good, now let's talk about what decides whether a farm survives: prices, weather and who owns the supermarkets. I'd make a dry joke about all the AI conferences we sat through.
S0.think: It'd mean very little for me beyond using the chat tool for subsidy forms. I'd be slightly disappointed, because I hoped something would finally take the paperwork off my desk.
S0.do: Carries on with the same staff, rotation and autosteer. Pays a few hundred a year for a farm management app once the farmers' association has tested it.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a forecast that says nothing much this week.
S0.quote: If AI had sorted only that, I'd have called it a success.
S0.fieldNote: Omar's measure of AI is very practical: whether it clears the spring scheme forms that he and Ruth argue over. He's secure, owns the land and adopts only what neighbours have proven. His first public instinct is to steer the talk back to prices and supermarket power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, if I were a betting man. Which I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need a fair share of whatever savings these tools make, not just the machinery dealers and the processors. At the association I'd push for a shared testing programme, so small farms can see what works before they spend. That's how we did it with the autosteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine. I'm the kind who waits two seasons and then buys the thing that works, and I can afford to. My worry is the people further down: the contract milkers and the lads who drive for contractors. Some of those jobs will shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever trials the association ran and I'd go and stand in my neighbour Petra's field when she got a weeding robot. If it worked for her two seasons running, I'd buy one, maybe forty or fifty thousand, out of savings rather than a loan. I'd send Sami on a course for running it, paid by the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. There's a bit of excitement in it, if I'm honest, as long as I'm not the one going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the people further down. Who do you actually know in that spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who does relief milking round six farms. He's good, but if half those farms go robotic, he's down to three. I'd ring him and say you're welcome here, but I can't give him five days, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you say the same thing at the association as you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. At the association I say we need public money for retraining. At home I say I'm glad I'm fifty-eight and not thirty. Both are true.

S1.say: I'd say farmers need a fair share of the savings these tools make, not just dealers and processors. I'd push the association for shared trials so small farms can see what works before spending.
S1.think: It's mostly fine for me, as I can wait two seasons and then afford the thing that works. My worry is relief milkers and contractors' drivers whose work will shrink.
S1.do: Joins the association's trials and watches a neighbour's weeding robot for two seasons. Then buys one for roughly forty to fifty thousand out of savings and pays for his young worker to train on it.
S1.feel: Mostly calm with a little excitement, as long as he isn't the first to try it.
S1.quote: At home I say I'm glad I'm fifty-eight and not thirty. Both are true.
S1.fieldNote: He's the classic steady adopter: watch the neighbour, then buy with cash. His concern for others is real and specific (Marek the relief milker) but it doesn't threaten him. He openly admits two slightly different lines in public and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's two harvests from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public problem and it needs a public answer, fast: income support, rules on who owns the robots, protection for rural jobs. At the association we'd call an emergency meeting. I'd be one of the people saying don't panic, but don't wait either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure what it means and that's what bothers me. If robots can do Dev's job and mine, who's buying the beef and at what price? The land's still ours, so we won't starve, but I couldn't tell you what Long Acre is worth in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be nothing big, because I don't buy what nobody's tested. I'd hold the savings, put off the new shed we'd planned, about eighty thousand, and wait to see what the machines really do on a farm like ours. I'd spend the time on the association, lobbying for support for workers like Dev and Marek. And I'd tell Dev his job is safe as long as I own the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a hailstorm warning two days before harvest, when you can't get the crop in any faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody's tested it. What does having only two years change for someone like you, who waits for proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It breaks my method. My whole way is to watch it work on someone else's farm first. With two years, by the time it's proven on Petra's place, it's already here. I'd be choosing in the dark, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You promised Dev his job is safe. Is that a promise you could keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, if the beef price drops through the floor. But I could keep it for a few years out of savings, and I would. He's been here eleven years. I'd rather lose money than look at him in the yard and say a machine's cheaper.

S2.say: I'd say this is a public problem needing a fast public answer: income support, rules on who owns the robots, and protection for rural jobs. At the association I'd say don't panic, but don't wait either.
S2.think: I don't really know what it means, and that's what bothers me. The land is ours so we won't starve, but I couldn't say what the farm is worth or who buys the beef at what price.
S2.do: Holds his savings and postpones a planned eighty-thousand shed while he waits to see real results. Lobbies through the farmers' association for workers' support, and promises his stockman a job for as long as he owns the farm.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a hail warning two days before harvest when the crop can't come in any faster.
S2.quote: With two years, by the time it's proven on Petra's place, it's already here.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning breaks his way of deciding, which is to wait for proof on a neighbour's farm. He's financially safe but genuinely unsure what his land and beef are worth in that world. His loyalty to Dev is concrete and he'd pay for it from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. That's two or three harvests of watching, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a short window and the association should use it: shared machines, a training fund, and a seat at the table when the rules get written. I'd say small farms can survive this if they buy together. I'd be on the radio if they asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a lot better than with two years. I'd get to see it work, which is all I ever ask. And I'd be sixty-three when it lands, which is close enough to stopping that the real question is what we leave Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Ruth and Lena and talk about whether she wants the farm, with robots or without. I'd watch the first trials on the bigger farms, then buy into a shared machinery group around year three. I'd also pay for Dev to do a robot maintenance course, so he's the one keeping them running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. Like a long dry spell you can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena at that kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you don't have to take this on. You've got a good job and people will still want a vet who can put her arm in a cow. But if you want the land, we'll set it up so the machines work for you, not the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd hold off on the shed. Does that change with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still hold it a year. Then, if the trials looked good, I'd build it differently, wider doors for machines and a charging bay instead of a feed passage. That's what five years buys you: you can build for the thing that's coming.

S3.say: I'd say the association should use the short window for shared machines, a training fund and a seat at the table on the rules. Small farms can survive this if they buy together.
S3.think: I'd feel much better than with two years, because I'd get to see it work first. At sixty-three when it lands, the real question is what we leave our daughter.
S3.do: Talks with his partner and daughter in the first year about whether she wants the farm. Joins a shared machinery group around year three after watching trials, and pays for his stockman to train in robot maintenance.
S3.feel: Uneasy but workable, like a long dry spell he can plan around.
S3.quote: That's what five years buys you: you can build for the thing that's coming.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years restore his preferred way of acting: watch, then buy. His thoughts shift to succession and what Lena inherits. The shed detail shows how practically he thinks about time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. Lena would be in her forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse to get this wrong. Ten years is time for training, time for proper rules, time for the association to make sure farmers own the machines and not some company in another country. I'd say it at every meeting I'm still invited to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable. I'd watch the robots get proven, buy the good ones when I'm ready and step back at sixty-five as planned. The bit I'd think about at night is Jonas, actually, because software sounds like the job they come for first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. I'd ease off on schedule, start handing more of the decisions to Lena around sixty-two if she wants it, and buy machines once they'd had a few seasons elsewhere. I'd also tell Jonas to think hard about his next move while he has ten years to make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, more or less. This one feels like something a family can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonas. What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't be proud, go and learn the thing that's replacing you before it does. He'd roll his eyes, because he thinks I'm the one who's behind. He's probably right about that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to do while you still have the farm as it is now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One more harvest week the old way, with everyone eating sandwiches standing up at midnight. I'd make sure Dev and Sami were there, and Lena if she could get away. Then I'd let the machines have it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves no excuse to get this wrong: time for training, proper rules and for farmers to own the machines rather than a company abroad.
S4.think: It's comfortable for me, as I'd buy proven machines and step back at sixty-five as planned. What I'd think about at night is my son, because software sounds like the job they come for first.
S4.do: Carries on and eases off on schedule, handing more decisions to his daughter from about sixty-two if she wants them. Buys machines after a few seasons of proof elsewhere and urges his son to plan his next move.
S4.feel: More or less calm, as it feels like something a family can plan for.
S4.quote: One more harvest week the old way, with everyone eating sandwiches standing up at midnight.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits his pace perfectly, so his own mood is calm. The worry moves to his son in software, which flips the usual picture of the farmer as the one at risk. His wish for one last old-style harvest shows the attachment underneath the practical talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it takes away the one thing I rely on, which is time to watch. What would help is a public testing programme for farm robots, run by people with no machines to sell, plus real support for workers like Dev. Give me honest results and I'll make good decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the robots. Everybody asks whether they'll take the jobs. I want to know whose name is on the paperwork, because whoever owns them owns the farm in the end.

headlineQuote: Everybody asks whether they'll take the jobs. I want to know whose name is on the paperwork, because whoever owns them owns the farm in the end.
portrait: Omar Weber, 58, farms 400 hectares of beef cattle, wheat and canola with his partner Ruth on land his grandfather bought, and employs three people. He is a careful adopter who waits for neighbours to prove a machine for two seasons before he buys it with cash, and he sits on the board of a regional farmers' association that pushes for fair contracts. In the mild pictures he is calm and practical. In the two-year AGI picture his method of waiting for proof breaks and he becomes anxious, holding his savings and lobbying for workers. With five or ten years he relaxes, plans succession with his daughter and worries more about his son's software job than his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it takes away the time he relies on to watch new machines prove themselves.
whatWouldHelp: A public testing programme for farm robots run by people with nothing to sell, plus real support for workers like his stockman Dev.
